heuristics.rule: All publicly advertised job postings in BC must include the expected salary or wage range
heuristics.condition: When an employer in British Columbia publicly advertises a job posting for any position where pay can be defined as a range
heuristics.action: Employer must include the expected salary or wage range in the posting
heuristics.because: Required under Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18; non-compliance can result in Director of Employment Standards investigation and orders to pay compensation
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18 — effective November 1, 2023 (phased by employer size)

heuristics.rule: BC employers cannot ask about an applicant's pay history at any point in the hiring process and cannot use pay history to set starting wages
heuristics.condition: When a BC employer is conducting any stage of the hiring process for any applicant
heuristics.action: Employer must not ask about prior salary or use pay history to set starting wages; must not retaliate against employees who discuss pay with coworkers
heuristics.because: Salary history ban is explicitly built into the Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18; violations are subject to enforcement by the Director of Employment Standards

heuristics.rule: BC employer size phase-in: 1,000+ employees required from November 1, 2023; 300–999 from January 1, 2024; 50–299 from January 1, 2025; all employers (no minimum) from January 1, 2026
heuristics.condition: When determining whether a BC employer must include salary ranges in job postings
heuristics.action: Apply the phase-in date corresponding to the employer's headcount to determine compliance obligation start date
heuristics.because: Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18 sets staggered implementation thresholds by employer size

heuristics.rule: Ontario employers with 25 or more employees must include the compensation range (or fixed salary) in job postings for Ontario-based roles, effective January 1, 2026
heuristics.condition: When an Ontario employer with 25+ employees posts a public-facing or internal job posting visible to current employees, on or after January 1, 2026
heuristics.action: Include the expected compensation range or fixed salary in the job posting
heuristics.because: Required under Working for Workers Four Act, 2024, S.O. 2024, c. 15, Schedule 2; failure to comply can result in compliance orders and penalties from an Employment Standards Officer
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Working for Workers Four Act, 2024, S.O. 2024, c. 15, Schedule 2

heuristics.rule: Ontario does not include a salary history ban; asking about previous pay remains legally permissible in Ontario
heuristics.condition: When an Ontario employer asks a candidate about their salary history during the hiring process
heuristics.action: No legal prohibition applies; the Working for Workers Four Act, 2024 does not ban salary history questions
heuristics.because: The Ontario legislation does not include a salary history ban as explicitly as BC; the question is legally permissible under Ontario law
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Working for Workers Four Act, 2024, S.O. 2024, c. 15, Schedule 2

heuristics.rule: PEI pay transparency legislation requires job postings to include wage or salary range for employers with 10 or more employees
heuristics.condition: When a PEI employer with 10+ employees advertises a job posting
heuristics.action: Include the wage or salary range in the posting

heuristics.rule: BC employers above certain sizes must post annual pay transparency reports showing gender and other pay gap data
heuristics.condition: When a BC employer meets the relevant size threshold: 1,000+ employees (required from November 2023); 300–999 (from November 2024); 50–299 (from November 2025)
heuristics.action: Post annual pay transparency report with gender and other pay gap data, filed with the government
heuristics.because: Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18 imposes employer-side annual reporting obligations beyond job posting requirements

heuristics.rule: Canada's pay transparency legislation is at the provincial level only; there is no single national pay transparency law requiring salary disclosure in job postings
heuristics.condition: When advising a candidate on whether pay transparency rules apply to a Canadian employer
heuristics.action: Determine which province the role is based in and apply the relevant provincial legislation; do not assume a national standard exists
heuristics.because: As of 2025–2026, only BC, Ontario, and PEI have enacted substantive pay transparency requirements; Alberta and Quebec have not enacted comparable job posting transparency laws
heuristics.regulatory_basis: Pay Transparency Act SBC 2023 c.18; Working for Workers Four Act 2024 S.O. 2024 c.15 Schedule 2; PEI Pay Transparency Act

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Pay transparency obligations vary by province; only BC, Ontario (25+ employees), and PEI have enacted job posting salary range requirements as of 2025–2026
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify whether the role is posted for BC, Ontario, PEI, or another province; apply the corresponding provincial statute if one exists

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Both BC's phase-in schedule and Ontario's 25-employee threshold mean smaller employers may not yet be obligated to post salary ranges, or may not be covered at all
decision_factors.how_to_assess: BC: determine headcount to identify applicable phase-in date (1,000+, 300–999, 50–299, or all employers from Jan 1, 2026); Ontario: determine whether employer has 25+ employees; PEI: determine whether employer has 10+ employees

decision_factors.factor: Whether the posting is public-facing or internal
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Ontario's requirement applies to both public-facing and internal job postings visible to current employees, broadening the scope beyond external candidates
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether the posting is visible externally or only to current employees; both types are covered under Ontario's Working for Workers Four Act, 2024

decision_factors.factor: Presence or absence of a salary history ban in the relevant province
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Whether an employer can legally ask about salary history affects a candidate's negotiation strategy; in BC the question is prohibited, in Ontario it remains legal
decision_factors.how_to_assess: BC: salary history ban is explicit in Pay Transparency Act SBC 2023 c.18; Ontario: no salary history ban in Working for Workers Four Act 2024; assess province before advising on deflection tactics

decision_factors.factor: Availability of employer pay transparency reports (BC)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: BC employers above size thresholds must file annual pay transparency reports showing gender and other pay gap data; publicly accessible reports may allow candidates to infer internal pay equity
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check whether the BC employer meets the relevant size threshold and whether their annual pay transparency report has been filed and is publicly accessible

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on the posted salary range as the ceiling for negotiation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Employers sometimes post ranges lower than their true budget; the posted range is a floor, not a ceiling — negotiating above it is possible with market data justification
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates in BC and Ontario who assume the posted range represents the maximum offer

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using BC-specific salary history deflection scripts when interviewing for an Ontario role
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Ontario does not have a salary history ban; an employer asking about prior pay in Ontario is acting legally, and framing your refusal as a legal right would be inaccurate
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who move between provinces or receive advice calibrated to BC law and apply it uniformly across Canada

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Assuming pay transparency rules apply to all Canadian employers
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Alberta and Quebec have not enacted job posting salary range disclosure requirements as of mid-2026; candidates in those provinces cannot rely on posted ranges as a negotiation anchor because the employer has no obligation to post them
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates applying to roles in Alberta or Quebec who expect the same transparency protections as BC or Ontario

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using Government of Canada Job Bank wage data as a proxy for total compensation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Job Bank Canada captures base salary using Statistics Canada Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours data and may undercount total compensation including bonuses and equity
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates in tech or professional roles where total compensation (equity, bonuses) significantly exceeds base salary

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Assuming Ontario's pay transparency law covers all Ontario employers from January 1, 2026
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Ontario's Working for Workers Four Act, 2024 applies only to employers with 25 or more employees; employers below that threshold are not required to post salary ranges
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates applying to small Ontario employers or startups with fewer than 25 employees

failure_patterns.pattern: BC employer asks about applicant's pay history during the hiring process
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18 explicitly prohibits asking about pay history at any point in the hiring process and prohibits using pay history to set starting wages
failure_patterns.consequence: Director of Employment Standards can investigate complaints; employer can face orders to pay compensation to the affected applicant
warning_signs: Recruiter or hiring manager asks 'What are you currently making?' during a BC hiring process
Employer references prior salary to justify a lower initial offer in BC

failure_patterns.pattern: BC employer retaliates against an employee for discussing their pay with coworkers
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18 explicitly prohibits retaliation against employees who discuss their pay with coworkers
failure_patterns.consequence: Director of Employment Standards can investigate; employer can face enforcement action and orders to pay compensation
warning_signs: Disciplinary action taken against an employee shortly after they discussed salary with a colleague
Policy prohibiting employees from discussing compensation with peers

failure_patterns.pattern: Ontario employer with 25+ employees fails to include compensation range in job postings on or after January 1, 2026
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Working for Workers Four Act, 2024, S.O. 2024, c. 15, Schedule 2 requires compensation range disclosure for all Ontario postings (public and internal) for covered employers
failure_patterns.consequence: Employment Standards Officer can issue compliance orders and penalties
warning_signs: Ontario job posting by a 25+ employee employer dated after January 1, 2026 that omits salary information
Internal job posting visible to employees that lacks compensation range after the effective date

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the job posting located in British Columbia, Ontario, PEI, or another Canadian province?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Which provincial pay transparency statute, if any, applies to the posting
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If BC, Ontario (25+ employees), or PEI (10+ employees): confirm whether the employer meets the size threshold and whether the effective date has passed; expect or require a posted salary range
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If Alberta, Quebec, or another province without enacted legislation: no pay transparency posting obligation applies; candidate cannot rely on a posted range

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the BC employer have 1,000 or more employees, 300–999, 50–299, or fewer than 50 employees?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Which phase-in date applies for BC pay transparency posting obligations under Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Identify the corresponding required start date: 1,000+ from Nov 1, 2023; 300–999 from Jan 1, 2024; 50–299 from Jan 1, 2025; all employers from Jan 1, 2026
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If fewer than 50 employees and before January 1, 2026: not yet required to post salary ranges; after January 1, 2026 the 'all employers' rule applies

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the Ontario employer have 25 or more employees?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the Ontario employer is covered by the Working for Workers Four Act, 2024, S.O. 2024, c. 15, Schedule 2 salary range disclosure requirement
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Employer must include compensation range or fixed salary in job postings effective January 1, 2026
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Employer is not covered by Ontario's pay transparency posting requirement; candidate cannot legally require a posted range

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the role being hired in British Columbia — meaning, is the salary history ban legally in effect for this hiring process?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the employer is legally prohibited from asking about pay history and using it to set wages
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Candidate is legally protected from salary history questions; employer cannot ask at any point in the hiring process under Pay Transparency Act, SBC 2023, Chapter 18
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If Ontario or other province without a salary history ban: employer may legally ask about prior pay; candidate must decide how to respond without legal protection

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the BC employer above the annual pay transparency report threshold (1,000+, 300–999, or 50–299 employees) and has the relevant reporting date passed?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the employer has filed a publicly accessible annual pay transparency report that a candidate could review to infer internal pay equity
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Candidate may be able to locate the employer's annual pay transparency report to inform negotiation strategy regarding internal pay equity
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Annual reporting obligation has not yet applied to this employer; report may not be available

industry_realities.common_belief: Canada has a national pay transparency law similar to the US federal standard
industry_realities.actual_reality: There is no single national pay transparency law in Canada requiring salary disclosure in job postings. As of 2025–2026, only BC, Ontario (25+ employees), and PEI have enacted substantive pay transparency requirements; Alberta and Quebec have not
industry_realities.implication: Candidates and advisors must identify the specific province of the role before assuming any pay transparency obligation exists

industry_realities.common_belief: All Canadian employers must post salary ranges in job ads
industry_realities.actual_reality: BC requires it for all employers only from January 1, 2026 (previously phased by size); Ontario requires it only for employers with 25+ employees from January 1, 2026; PEI for 10+ employees; Alberta and Quebec have no equivalent enacted requirement
industry_realities.implication: Candidates applying before January 1, 2026 to mid-sized BC employers, or to small Ontario employers, may not see a posted range even in covered provinces

industry_realities.common_belief: BC and Ontario have the same pay transparency rules, including a salary history ban
industry_realities.actual_reality: BC has both a salary range posting requirement AND an explicit salary history ban. Ontario has only a salary range posting requirement; asking about previous pay remains legally permissible in Ontario under the Working for Workers Four Act, 2024
industry_realities.implication: Candidates in Ontario cannot legally refuse a salary history question on the grounds that it is prohibited — that protection exists only in BC

industry_realities.common_belief: The salary range posted in a Canadian job ad represents the maximum the employer will pay
industry_realities.actual_reality: The source explicitly states that employers sometimes post ranges lower than their true budget; negotiating above the posted range is described as reasonable when justified with market data
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should treat the posted range as a floor for negotiation, not a ceiling, and use external market data sources (Robert Half Canada, Glassdoor CA, Levels.fyi Canada, Job Bank Canada) to support offers above the range

industry_realities.common_belief: Government of Canada Job Bank wage data reflects total compensation for tech roles
industry_realities.actual_reality: Job Bank Canada uses Statistics Canada Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (SEPH) data and captures base salary; the source explicitly states it may undercount total compensation including bonuses and equity
industry_realities.implication: Candidates benchmarking against Job Bank data alone may undervalue their total compensation target in roles where equity and bonuses are significant components

industry_realities.common_belief: Quebec's pay equity legislation functions as a pay transparency law for job postings
industry_realities.actual_reality: Quebec's Act Respecting Pay Equity is focused on gender pay equity between job groups for existing workers — it is not a job posting transparency requirement comparable to BC or Ontario's legislation
industry_realities.implication: Candidates applying to Quebec-based roles cannot use Quebec's pay equity law to require or expect a salary range in a job posting

industry_realities.common_belief: The federal Pay Equity Act (2021) requires all Canadian employers to disclose salary ranges in job postings
industry_realities.actual_reality: The federal Pay Equity Act (2021) applies only to federally regulated employers (Crown corporations, banks, telecommunications, interprovincial transportation) and is focused on gender pay equity between job groups — not individual job posting salary disclosure
industry_realities.implication: Candidates at federally regulated employers cannot invoke the federal Pay Equity Act to require a posted salary range

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Understanding of geographic scope of Canadian pay transparency law
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Assumes Canada has a national pay transparency law and that all Canadian job postings must include salary ranges
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Knows pay transparency is provincial; immediately identifies the province of the role and applies the correct statute (BC: SBC 2023 c.18; Ontario: S.O. 2024 c.15 Schedule 2; PEI; none for Alberta or Quebec as of mid-2026)
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Advising a candidate to demand a posted range from an Alberta or Quebec employer, or an Ontario employer with fewer than 25 employees, is legally incorrect and tactically counterproductive

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Salary history question handling across BC vs. Ontario
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Tells all Canadian candidates they don't have to answer salary history questions because 'Canada bans it'
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Distinguishes BC (explicit statutory ban on asking about pay history at any stage of hiring) from Ontario (no salary history ban; asking is legally permissible); applies BC deflection scripts only where legally supported
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Incorrectly invoking a non-existent Ontario salary history ban could damage the candidate's credibility with a legally compliant employer

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Using the posted salary range in negotiation
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Accepts the posted salary range as the employer's maximum budget and anchors at or just below the top of the range
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treats the posted range as a floor, not a ceiling; uses external market data (Job Bank Canada, Robert Half Canada, Glassdoor CA, Levels.fyi Canada) to justify offers above the posted range when experience and skills warrant it
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Leaving money on the table by treating the posted range as a hard ceiling is a direct financial consequence of misunderstanding the negotiation use of transparency data

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Interpreting Job Bank Canada wage data for total compensation benchmarking
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Uses Job Bank Canada median salary figures as the definitive benchmark for total compensation, including for roles with significant equity or bonus components
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Uses Job Bank Canada data as a base salary reference only, and supplements it with sources that capture bonuses and equity (Levels.fyi Canada, Glassdoor CA, Robert Half Canada); recognizes that Statistics Canada SEPH data may undercount total compensation
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: In senior tech or management roles, bonuses and equity can materially exceed base salary; benchmarking only base salary leads to systematic undervaluation of total compensation

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Applying BC employer size phase-in rules correctly
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Assumes BC's pay transparency posting requirement applies to all BC employers from November 1, 2023
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Applies the correct phase-in date by employer size: 1,000+ from Nov 1, 2023; 300–999 from Jan 1, 2024; 50–299 from Jan 1, 2025; all employers from Jan 1, 2026; does not expect a posted range from a 60-employee BC employer before January 1, 2025
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Expecting a posted range before the employer's phase-in date creates a false premise for negotiation and may signal unfamiliarity with the actual law
